item.title: Remembering what is: Indigenising reflections of an urban landscape
item.description:
Nicolette Duncan
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261503451
Melbourne city as it exists today is a colonial project with a history of destruction, exclusion and denial of local First Nations sovereignty on Wurundjeri Country. This fact is taken for granted in the urban environment today whereby acknowledgement of Wurundjeri presence in this location is presented as in the past, with little explanation or accountability offered as to the transition from Wurundjeri custodianship of Country to present modern urbanity. Country, as understood by Wurundjeri people, extends beyond the landscape to include social, temporal and spiritual dimensions. Recent efforts to reconcile Melbourne’s colonial history reflect these multiple dimensions. In this brief article, I reflect on place-making and historical narrative in urban Melbourne on Wurundjeri Country from a non-Indigenous perspective. To combat narrow colonial understandings of Melbourne’s history, and complement reconciliatory efforts, Country is discussed as a multidimensional conceptual framework which could be applied to encourage a greater sense of appreciation for Wurundjeri Country, the past, and an inclusive social future on common ground.

item.title: Companions, not just services: What do experiences of time teach us about urban vegetation?
item.description:
Soledad Martínez Rodríguez
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261503483
Urban nature literature often describes urban vegetation in terms of its ‘ecosystem services’ such as carbon sequestration, air filtering, noise reduction and soil permeability, among others. Studies also note that green spaces foster social cohesion by providing places for social encounters and activities. Nevertheless, the bodily and sensorial relationships that urban dwellers create with urban vegetation are overlooked within these accounts. From an anthropological view that understands places as human and other-than-human entanglements, urban dwellers’ relationships with vegetation are poorly captured by the more transactional concept of ‘ecosystem services’. In this commentary, I bring to light shared temporalities between urban walkers and vegetation to argue for a closer look at the intertwined complexities of human and more-than-human cohabitation. Based on ethnographic research in Osorno, a small city in southern Chile – often referred to as a ‘green city’ because of its abundant vegetation – I delve into the experiences and narratives that emerge from people’s everyday contact with urban vegetation through their everyday journeys on foot. They invite us to rethink what urban nature does to urban places and what it means for these walkers, which is more than just providing humans with some ‘services’. Here, I show how everyday encounters with urban vegetation invite people to experience time differently. People can attune to more-than-human temporalities through senses and affects, allowing them to recall past times and also be part of a cyclical time we – humans and other-than-humans – all share.

item.title: Time as a commons: Collective temporal practices and the making of urban care infrastructures
item.description:
Maro Pantazidou
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261503494
The contemporary care crisis has prompted a surge of scholarly attention to urban care commons and bottom-up care infrastructures, with particular emphasis on their socio-spatial dynamics. By contrast, the temporal dynamics through which such formations are sustained have received limited attention. While previous research has engaged urban and institutional temporalities in relation to processes of commoning, the commoning of time itself remains underexplored as a pathway towards urban transformation. This article turns to the urban co-production of time, focusing on the temporal patterns that sustain one of the largest self-organised collective kitchens in crisis-ridden central Athens. The kitchen mobilises dozens of residents in daily food provisioning and redistribution, preparing and sharing hundreds of warm meals 6 days a week. The scale and continuity of the initiative provide a unique empirical lens for understanding the organisational and meaning-making practices, at the temporal level, that make informal urban care infrastructures possible. Drawing on 10 months of ethnographic fieldwork, the article illuminates both the temporal resources (clock-time hours) and the temporal orientations (valuations of time beyond clock-time) that underpin alternative arrangements of social provisioning. The findings introduce the concept of collective time work to describe how otherwise temporally fragmented urban communities pool time and remake temporal norms to create cohesive community care. Conceptually, the article advances time as a relational, co-produced good, rather than an individually managed resource, to foreground the politics of time as a vital vector for transforming how care is organised and sustained in cities.

item.title: Provisioning otherwise: Platform co-operatives and the reworking of platform urbanism
item.description:
Jun Zhang
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261505798
Urban life is increasingly organised through platforms, but platform urbanism has largely been understood through corporate intermediation, extraction and regulation. This article asks what becomes visible when platformisation is approached instead through the politics of provision. Drawing on 31 semi-structured interviews across a translocal platform co-operative ecosystem, it examines how co-operatively governed digital infrastructures make shared provision workable across places. The article develops platformed mutual provisioning to describe a recursive process through which dispersed capacities are assembled around situated needs, extended through federation and kept collectively governable through maintenance, democratic learning and data stewardship. The findings show that platform co-operatives matter less as ownership alternatives in themselves than as fragile experiments in organising the coordinating capacities on which food systems, logistics and civic economies increasingly depend. Their significance lies in keeping those capacities revisable as they become infrastructural to everyday provision. The article argues that this opens a wider politics of co-operative infrastructural urbanism, in which digital urbanisation is judged not by growth or technological novelty, but by whether the power to coordinate provision remains answerable to those who depend upon it.

item.title: Healthcare real estate and urban infrastructure: between public good and financial asset
item.description:
Jenny Zhenyi Huang, Sotiris Tsolacos
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261497185
In contemporary urbanism, healthcare real estate plays the dual role of essential social infrastructure and financial asset. On the one hand, healthcare real estate functions as a vital form of social infrastructure, shaping patterns of accessibility, belonging, and resilience in cities. On the other hand, it is increasingly governed as a financial asset through public-private partnerships (PPPs), real estate investment trusts (REITs), and institutional investment. This article conceptualises healthcare real estate as a form of financialised social infrastructure situated at the intersection of public service provision, financial investment, and urban governance. Drawing on evidence from the UK healthcare estate, the article examines how healthcare real estate has become increasingly embedded within circuits of capital accumulation and integrated into broader processes of financialised urbanism. The analysis demonstrates that financialisation has reshaped the financing and governance of healthcare real estate, expanding the role of institutional investors and private capital and reinforcing investment logics within healthcare provision. While these developments can mobilise capital for infrastructure investment and estate modernisation, they may also generate governance challenges relating to ownership, accountability, accessibility, and spatial equity. The article contributes to urban studies by advancing understanding of healthcare real estate as a form of financialised social infrastructure and examining its implications for health equity and sustainable urban development. It further explores the potential of impact investment as a mechanism for reconciling financial and social objectives, highlighting the importance of impact evaluation frameworks in aligning private capital with broader social and spatial outcomes.

item.title: Blind spots of state spatial selectivity: The left-behind secondary cities in Chinese mega-regionalisation
item.description:
Yizhao Du, Rodrigo V. Cardoso, Roberto Rocco
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261498005
Chinese intra-regional unevenness remains unresolved, despite mega-regionalisation being promoted as the main instrument of state spatial selectivity aimed at alleviating polarisation and peripheralisation in secondary cities. We argue that a largely overlooked intermediate stage of such processes is partly responsible for the uneven outcomes of mega-regionalisation in tackling these challenges. This stage bridges mega-regional visions initiated by top-level authorities and practical interventions at the local scale, organised in action plans that determine relations between core and secondary cities by state actors at the provincial level. We select three representative Chinese mega-regions and examine the yearly reports from 2006 to 2024 of their provincial governments (acting as mega-regional coordinators) to summarise the various mechanisms and periodic trends of these plans through the analytical lens of historical institutionalism. We find that the intermediate stage, focused on spatial reconfiguration, redistribution of urban functions, and improving regional accessibility, emphasises cores as the driving force, leaving blind spots that allow only a few secondary cities to integrate and benefit from mega-regionalisation, whereas many more are further polarised and peripheralised. This is evidenced in all cases despite their different trends in specific action plans. We highlight the impact of intermediate-stage action plans on secondary cities to extend spatial selectivity theory to multi-scalar state-led regionalisation processes and call for policy and governance attention to intermediate-stage coordination mechanisms that allow representation of secondary cities in mega-regional planning.

item.title: Veganism in the city: Capitalist assimilation or multispecies resistance?
item.description:
Corey Lee Wrenn
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261499626
Cities are spaces in which consumerism, culture, and protest must often comingle. Often concentrated in urban spaces, veganism—which advocates alternative consumption, multispecies multiculturalism, and resistance to harmful foodways and unequal multispecies relationships—offers an interesting case study of urban consumerist dynamics. Using semiotic analysis of signs, posted menus, advertisements, and window displays collected between 2021 and 2022 in one university town in southeast England, it is considered how veganism might be able to persist, perhaps even thrive, in capital-serving cityscapes. Findings suggest that veganism is strained by the marketplace function of the city. Veganism is reduced to a form of consumption that aligns with capitalist interests, and anti-speciesist representations of veganism are lacking. Yet, this study also considers if the prevalence of vegan signage could be moderately subversive in normalizing veganism. These complexities are considered in the context of geographical and sociological research on cities as sites of both corporate co-optation of protest and social change.

item.title: Solidarity kitchens and community gardens: Commoning practices of care in urban peripheries
item.description:
Renata Motta, Anne Cathrin Ziegler, Maria Eugênia Trombini
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261504189
This article examines urban food commons by tracing the emergence of food cultivation and preparation initiatives in urban peripheries, including occupied and contested territories. Nutritional studies often classify urban occupations and housing projects as food deserts or food swamps. Drawing on feminist political ecology, decolonial feminist perspectives on urban commons and care and Black Food Geographies, our research reframes these environments not as deficient but as care infrastructures where commoning practices among plants, people and place are enacted. The research focuses on community gardens and solidarity kitchens in the Brazilian metropolitan region of Belo Horizonte, based on fieldwork and focus groups with members from a state–society network of food activists that have shaped the alternative food system in Belo Horizonte in the last three decades. Beyond the binary of ‘social fixes’ for capitalist urbanisation and localised prefigurative spaces of post-capitalist difference, we treat community gardens and kitchens as spaces for (re)organising social reproduction, reproducing a socio-natural network and providing care that can unlock transformative potentialities. Furthermore, we claim that these urban food commons sparked renewed state commitment, transforming not only the political ecology of food and the urban landscape in the peripheries of Belo Horizonte but also state policies, aiming at promoting state-commons. Tensions remain, however, considering the relationships between autonomy in commoning practices and the state. Our article contributes to discussions of urban food commons by examining their relational dynamics with the state.
